t.4.12.1: Having heard these well-spoken words of Sugrīva, the greatly splendid Rāma took up his bow in order to inspire confidence.
t.4.12.2: He, the bestower of honour, took up his terrible bow and a single arrow and, aiming at the sāla trees, let it fly, filling the directions with the twanging of the bowstring.
t.4.12.3: That gold-adorned arrow, loosed by the mighty one, pierced the seven sāla trees on the mountain slope and entered the earth.
t.4.12.4: Swift as it was, the arrow split the earth and plunged into it within a moment; then, flying out again in haste, it entered back into its own quiver.
t.4.12.5: Seeing those seven sāla trees pierced through by the force of Rāma's arrow, the bull among monkeys was overcome with the utmost wonder.
t.4.12.6: Supremely delighted, Sugrīva, his ornaments hanging down, fell to the ground with his head bowed before Rāghava, his palms joined in reverence.
t.4.12.7: Delighted by that deed, he spoke these words to Rāma, the knower of dharma, the foremost of all those skilled in weapons, the hero standing there.
t.4.12.8: O bull among men, with your arrows you are able to slay in battle all the gods, even together with Indra; how much more, then, Vālin, O lord!
t.4.12.10: Today my grief has departed, and today my joy is supreme, for I have gained you as a friend, you who are like great Indra and Varuṇa.
t.4.12.9: O Kākutstha, you who with a single arrow have pierced the seven great sāla trees, the mountain and the earth, who could stand against you at the forefront of battle?
t.4.12.12: Then the greatly wise Rāma, embracing Sugrīva, pleasing to behold, replied with words approved by Lakṣmaṇa.
t.4.12.11: This very day, O Kākutstha, for my sake, slay Vālin, that enemy in the form of a brother; see, I have joined my palms in supplication.
t.4.12.13: Let us go from here to Kiṣkindhā; go quickly on ahead, Sugrīva, and when you get there, challenge Vālin, who is a brother in name only.
t.4.12.14: All of them went swiftly to Kiṣkindhā, the city of Vālin, and, concealing themselves behind the trees, they stood in the dense forest.
t.4.12.15: Sugrīva, tightly girded, roared terribly in order to challenge Vālin, and with vehemence seemed to split the sky with his roars.
t.4.12.16: Hearing that roar of his brother, the mighty Vālī, enraged and greatly agitated, rushed forth like the sun from the slope of the western mountain.
t.4.12.17: Then there arose a most tumultuous battle between Vālin and Sugrīva, terrible like that of the two planets Budha and Aṅgāraka in the sky.
t.4.12.18: With palms like thunderbolts and with fists like the vajra, the two brothers, swooning with rage, struck each other in the battle.
t.4.12.19: Then Rāma, bow in hand, looked closely at the two of them, both heroes so alike to each other, like the two divine Aśvins.
t.4.12.20: Since Rāghava could not tell Sugrīva from Vālin, he did not resolve to release his death-dealing arrow.
t.4.12.21: Meanwhile Sugrīva, broken by that Vālin and not seeing Rāghava, his protector, fled to Ṛśyamūka.
t.4.12.22: Exhausted, his limbs drenched with blood, battered and broken by the blows, and pursued by Vālin in his wrath, he entered the great forest.
t.4.12.23: Seeing him enter the forest, Vālī, out of fear of the curse, then said, "You are indeed set free," and that mighty one turned back.
t.4.12.24: Rāghava too, together with his brother and with Hanumān, was coming to that very forest where the vānara Sugrīva was.
t.4.12.25: Seeing Rāma arrive together with Lakṣmaṇa, Sugrīva, filled with shame and gazing at the ground, spoke these piteous words.
t.4.12.26: Having told me, "Challenge him," and having shown me your prowess, and then having let me be struck down by the enemy, what is this that you have now done?
t.4.12.27: At that very moment, O Rāghava, you ought to have told me truthfully, 'I will not slay Vālin'; then I would not have set out from here.
t.4.12.28: As the great-souled Sugrīva was speaking thus, piteously and in a dejected voice, Rāghava spoke again.
t.4.12.30: In adornment, in dress, in stature and in gait, you, O Sugrīva, and Vālī are alike to each other.
t.4.12.29: Sugrīva, my dear, let your anger be put aside and let the reason be heard for which this arrow was not released by me.
t.4.12.31: In voice and in splendour, in glance, in prowess and in speech, O monkey, I cannot perceive any distinction between the two of you.
t.4.12.32: Then, O best of monkeys, bewildered by the likeness of your forms, I did not release my arrow of great speed, the destroyer of foes.
t.4.12.33: But within this very moment, behold Vālin in battle, struck down by me with a single arrow and writhing upon the surface of the earth.
t.4.12.34: O lord of the vānaras, make for yourself some mark of recognition, by which I may recognize you when you have entered into single combat.
t.4.12.35: O Lakṣmaṇa, uproot this blossoming gajapuṣpī creeper of auspicious marks and place it around the neck of the great-souled Sugrīva.
t.4.12.36: Then Lakṣmaṇa uprooted a gajapuṣpī creeper laden with flowers that had grown on the mountainside, and placed it around his neck.
t.4.12.37: With the creeper clinging to his neck, that glorious one shone like a cloud at twilight wreathed with a garland of cranes.
t.4.12.38: Shining in his form and heartened by Rāma's words, he went together with Rāma to Kiṣkindhā, which was guarded by Vālin.
